NRL Late Mail: Grand Final - Ioelu in for Watson; Graham steps up
Youngster Benaiah Ioelu has been added to the Roosters' six-man interchange bench for Sunday's grand final after Connor Watson was ruled out on Friday.
Watson suffered a head knock just one minute after coming on to the field in the preliminary final victory over the Dolphins on September 25 and was promptly ruled out of the remainder of the match.
With players typically placed into an 11-day stand-down period after a concussion, the Roosters sought clearance from an independent neurologist for Watson to line up in the grand final, which comes nine days after the head knock.
The request was denied and 22-year-old Ioelu comes into the 19 in his sixth game of the season and just the 18th of his career.
"Ultimately it came down to protocol and we stand by that," coach Trent Robinson said.
"Connor spoke to the group quite clearly about 'this is about the group' and he passed that on, and then the player who took his spot in the 19, Benaiah spoke about the love for Connor and what it means for his role coming into the team and that's what teams are about."

DCE eyeing slice of history in fairytale finale
Roosters playmaker Daly Cherry-Evans has opened up on his evolution as a player and a person as he looks to cap a fairytale farewell to the NRL.
The veteran will play his final game in the competition in Sunday's grand final, 15 years after he led Manly to the premiership in his rookie season.
Cherry-Evans was back in a decider two years later, winning the Clive Churchill Medal as his Sea Eagles went down to the Roosters.

It's been 13 years since he's played in a grand final and plenty has changed for the playmaker as he eyes a fairytale farewell before joining Hull FC next season.
"If you look at anyone who's 22 years old and fast forward to them as a 37-year-old, things change," Cherry-Evans said. "I'm a husband and a father now. I'm sure there are some mannerisms that have held true with my footy.
"I'm obviously more mature, so I have a better understanding of what the team needs. I was very instinctive as a young player coming through the grades. I didn't have a lot of structure around me; not that it wasn't getting coached into me, but my style of play and personality was just playing what I see.
"Over time I've become a halfback. For a long time I was a five-eighth wearing a number seven, and right now I'm probably a halfback wearing a number six."

Cherry-Evans took the NRL by storm in his rookie season and quickly developed into one of the best playmakers in the game.
While he now concedes he was a five-eighth playing in the No.7 jumper, he eventually developed into a ball-playing halfback with a dynamic running game and one of the best kicking boots in the business.
Representative honours quickly followed, Cherry-Evans making his Kangaroos debut just weeks after winning the 2011 grand final.
Daly Cherry-Evans celebrates milestone game in style
A maiden State of Origin appearance for Queensland followed in 2013 and he went on to captain his state while becoming the oldest player to feature in the interstate series.
The 2013 grand final, however, was the last time Cherry-Evans has featured on the first Sunday in October, with club success proving elusive.
The veteran acknowledges he eventually came to appreciate how tough it is to play for a premiership and is determined to make the most of one last shot at glory.
"Probably around year six to year 10 I started to realise how difficult it was to make finals, let alone a grand final," Cherry-Evans said.
"There were a couple of lean years there and it gives you a really strong appreciation for the times you do get to play in a finals series. It's definitely not lost on me how lucky I am to be playing in the grand final this weekend."
Cherry-Evans became the youngest halfback to win a premiership in the NRL era when he led Manly to glory in 2011 as a 22-year-old.
A win on Sunday will make him the oldest player in the NRL era to prevail in a grand final, eclipsing Cam Smith's record set in 2020. He will also be the oldest premiership winner since North Sydney's George Green won in 1922 as a 38-year-old.
Cherry-Evans will also set a new record for longest gap between premierships, surpassing Lote Tuqiri's mark of 14 years.

How a journey deep underground set Knights on path to NRL grand final
“It’s a hard-working area and you want to see that in your rugby league team, that’ll never change.”
That was Justin Holbrook outlining his vision for the Knights during his introductory press conference as coach last September.
A former Newcastle halfback who served as Andrew Johns’ backup and played alongside Danny Buderus, Matt Gidley and Robbie O’Davis, Holbrook has made it his mission to reconnect the team to its community.
Words, however, can ring hollow without tangible action.
Holbrook: "A big part of our fanbase is people who work in the mines"
On January 13, Holbrook’s 50th birthday, the Knights showed through actions how they plan to represent the Hunter.
The coach took the playing group down the Myuna Colliery mine to see firsthand how the region’s people live and work.
It was an eye-opening experience for the squad and the day the first steps were taken on a path that will culminate in Sunday’s grand final.
“It was pretty surreal,” veteran Tyson Frizell told NRL.com. “Mining is in the DNA of this town. Everyone wants to have a connection to their town and what better way than to go down there and genuinely understand what people go through and what they do for a living.
“Their days are spent with no technology, no social media and the enjoyment they get on a Monday morning is talking about how the Knights went on the weekend. To see that and hear it from the guys down there was a cool experience.”

Given they finished last year with the wooden spoon, few expected the Knights to be playing in a grand final just 12 months after Holbrook’s arrival.
The coach, however, was always confident of what this team could achieve and carries that same belief into Sunday’s decider against the Roosters at a sold-out Accor Stadium.
From that first trip down the mine shaft, the Knights have slowly built a wave of fan support that will reach a crescendo this weekend.
Grand Final emotions after 12-man win
More than 12,000 fans turned out for Wednesday’s open training session, thousands more will make the two-hour trip down the M1 to Accor Stadium and 25,000 supporters will pack into McDonald Jones Stadium to watch their team on the big screen.
It’s been impossible to avoid grand final fever across the Hunter throughout the past week, from the mines to the dairy farms and everywhere in between.
“Going down the mines was a real eye-opener,” forward Mat Croker, who grew up on a dairy farm, said. “We speak a lot about how this town has a mining culture and these blokes save up their money all week to come to a Knights game.
“Once we went down there, it drew a real connection for a lot of the boys. We’ve brought it up a fair bit this year. How we can make these people proud. These are people that have tougher lives than we’ve got as footy players.
“It’s our responsibility to make sure they have a good week by going out and performing well. A lot of them are having much better weeks now and I bet they are underground now talking about the grand final on Sunday.”
Beyond connecting with the community, the Knights have also made a concerted effort to rebuild their junior pathways.
Director of football Chris James was brought in with a mission to establish a pipeline between the region’s fertile nursery of juniors all the way through to the NRL team.
It’s a path Croker followed as a teenager, the Nabiac product captaining the Knights Harold Matthews and SG Ball teams as a teenager before progressing through Jersey Flegg, NSW Cup and eventually making his NRL debut in 2021.

Roosters v Knights: Watson ruled out; Graham rises for Phoenix
After 27 rounds and three pulsating weeks of finals, it all comes down to 80 minutes at Accor Stadium this Sunday to decide the 2026 NRL champions.
The pride of the Hunter taking on the boys from Bondi in an epic decider that no one saw coming and no one wants to miss.
The Knights have come from seventh spot to qualify for their first grand final since 2001 and are chasing just the third premiership in club history.
The Roosters are into their first decider since 2019 and will look to add a 16th premiership to one of the game's most glittering trophy cabinets.
In many ways the most unlikely of grand final pairings but also the most romantic as last year’s wooden spooners Newcastle look to complete a fairytale revival.
The last team to climb from the dungeon one year to decider the next was their opponents the Roosters, who dusted themselves off after a disastrous 2009 season to charge into the 2010 grand final, where they lost to the Dragons.
Do the underdogs have one more upset left in them or have they spent all their chips? All will be revealed on Sunday night at Accor Stadium in front of a heaving crowd befitting the occasion.
One play can define a season. These are the moments that matter. Don't miss a second of the action with kick-off at 7.30pm Sunday night live on Nine, 9Now and Sky Sports NZ.

Kiwis switch paves way for Gagai-Mitchell World Cup re-match
Dane Gagai V Latrell Mitchell Round 2 could kick start IRL Rugby League World Cup 2026 after the Knights centre was cleared to play for the Kiwis on the eve of the NRL grand final.
Gagai, who is aiming to complete a fairytale finish to his career with the Knights in Sunday's premiership decider against Sydney Roosters, has been granted permission to switch his international eligibility from Australia to New Zealand.
The 35 year-old, who is set to finish his NRL career at the Broncos, is now in line for a Kiwis call up and his first assignment could be opposite Mitchell in the World Cup opener at Allianz Stadium on October 15.
The pair went head-to-head - and toe-to-toe - in an explosive opening match of the NRL finals series which began Newcastle's march to an unlikely grand final appearance after being wooden spooners last season.
Vintage Gagai
Gagai has wound back the clock as the Knights have overcome Mitchell's Rabbitohs, the Warriors in New Zealand and minor premiers Penrith to earn a shot at history against the Roosters.
An International Rugby League Appeals Committee approved Gagai's application to change Tier 1 eligibility from Australia to New Zealand.
Gagai qualifies for New Zealand through his mother Tania and has represented his Ngāti Pikiāo heritage by playing for Māori All Stars since 2019.
He has previously played for Australia and was a member of the Kangaroos team which won the final of IRL Rugby League World Cup 2017.
Under IRL eligibility rules players who represent a Tier 1 nation – Australia, England and New Zealand – are unable to play for another Tier 1 nation. Gagai’s application was initially rejected on those grounds.
However, IRL recently permitted Kalyn Ponga to switch his international allegiances to New Zealand and AJ Brimson to play for England after both had represented Australia at the IRL World Cup Nines in 2019.

Changes to State of Origin eligibility rules also enabled Briton Nikora, Casey McLean and Addin Fonua-Blake to play in this year’s series despite not being eligible for Australia as they have represented New Zealand.
An IRL Appeals Committee accepted that Gagai, who has played 23 State of Origins for Queensland, had not been afforded the same opportunity.
Gagai has not played for Australia since 2018, and he was not selected in the preliminary 40-man squad for IRL Rugby League World Cup 2026.

Mates to rivals: Coaches put friendship aside in battle for glory
Trent Robinson didn't hesitate to pick up the phone in Justin Holbrook's darkest hour.
It's late 2023 and the rugby league world had just been blindsided by the news the Titans had sacked Holbrook and replaced him with Des Hasler.
Robinson was searching for an assistant and knew exactly what he was getting from a man who had previously served on his coaching staff before a successful stint in charge of St Helens that culminated in a Super League premiership.
Holbrook jumped at the chance to link up with his former mentor and quickly built one of the best attacking sides in the NRL.
Grand Final emotions after 12-man win
"It was 2014 when we first hired Justin as an assistant and it was a pretty easy choice to get him back in 2024 when the Titans didn't end as he wanted it to," Robinson said.
"He's always been a great coach. You look at his success through the junior grades and his demeanour, it's always been a real positive. There's a clear knowledge of footy and a good man in there so it was a pretty easy choice [to hire him]."

Two years on and the close mates are preparing to go head-to-head in Sunday's NRL grand final when the Roosters take on the Knights.
While many figured Holbrook would help turn Newcastle into a premiership contender, the pace of the turnaround has exceeded all expectations.
After finishing last in 2025 with the worst attack in the competition, the coach has unlocked attacking weapons all across the park.
Newcastle winger Dom Young has scored 23 tries this season, with fellow winger Greg Marzhew crossing for 24 tries, and is among the players who have been coached by both Holbrook and Robinson.
Dom-inating display from Young
Having spent 18 months with the Roosters before returning to the Knights midway through last season, the Englishman said the pair have vastly different personalities.
"They're very different coaches," Young said. "Justin is a bit more easy-going and a jokester who doesn't take things too seriously. Robbo is a bit more of a serious character.
"They're both good coaches and have different styles and ways of getting the best out of their players.
"Justin has been massive for us. The way he's brought it all together this year, the style of football we're playing and the way everyone's bought into it. He's been a really good coach for us."
The differences between the two men were on display at Thursday's Grand Final Press Conference.
Robinson was steely-eyed and focused on the task at hand. Holbrook was cracking jokes and soaking in the excitement of his first decider as a head coach.
Difference maker - Kalyn Ponga
"I've been this way all year," Holbrook said when asked about his jovial mood. "It's no different to the start of the finals series. We've been confident we could play well and win every week and we've faced some different challenges.
"I'm so happy for the playing group and how hard they've worked. We've earned our way to Sunday and I'm not going to change the way I am or the playing group."
Beneath the playful exterior lies a hard underbelly that has demanded excellence from his players.
A former Knight who was also part of the Roosters squad during their 2002 premiership season, Holbrook has placed an emphasis on ensuring his team reflects the hard-working nature of the community they represent.

Knights riding wave of support as fans take over Harbour Bridge
Injured Newcastle halfback Dylan Brown has declared Monday's takeover of the Sydney Harbour Bridge is just the beginning as excitement builds for the NRL Grand Final.
Hundreds of fans marched across the iconic Sydney site on Monday afternoon before descending on Campbells Cove for the official launch of Grand Final week.
The Knights have been riding a wave of fan support throughout the past couple of weeks to book a showdown with the Roosters at a sold-out Accor Stadium on Sunday.
With both their men's and women's sides qualifying for the grand final, plenty of Roosters fans also turned out for Monday's march to get behind their club's quest for dual premiership glory.
Game breaker: Sandon Smith's match-winning double
Brown watched from the sidelines last weekend as Newcastle qualified for their first decider since 2001 in front of a crowd of 57,000 fans heavily weighted in the Knights' favour.
Another convoy of Sid Fogg’s coaches will make the trip down the M1 this weekend for the sold-out clash at Accor Stadium and Brown said the players are determined to repay their fans with a drought-breaking victory.
"It makes you so happy to see all these fans here on a Monday afternoon," Brown said. "You can't not be happy when you're seeing your fans in a place they deserve to be.
"They've been very patient, spent 25 years waiting and we're here now. We've got one more job to do, nothing's finished yet so we ought to get it done."

Penrith and the Dolphins will face off in the State Championship to kickstart proceedings before the undefeated Roosters take on the Broncos in a rematch of last year’s epic NRLW grand final.
Brisbane are determined to send club legend Ali Brigginshaw out with another title while the Tricolours are out to avenge their defeat 12 months ago.
The Knights and Roosters will then take centre stage for the NRL decider with Justin Holbrook's men out to cap a fairytale rise from last year's wooden spoon to a title.
The Roosters are desperate to send veteran Daly Cherry-Evans out with a ring in his final game in the NRL as they chase their first title since 2019.
Roosters and Knights fans took over the Sydney Harbour Bridge on Monday afternoon for a fan march to kick off Grand Final Week.
Brown will miss the match after tearing his ACL in a Round 21 loss to the Tricolours, with former Rooster Sandon Smith starring since stepping into the No.7 jumper.
A New Zealand international, Brown has experienced some all-time atmospheres throughout his playing career and he's expecting Sunday night to climb straight to the top of the list.
"It will be a bit like the Pacific Championships," Brown said. "People have seen the Tongan games, it's going to be like that on Sunday. It will be a red sea of Knights fans and there will be a lot of flags flying.
"We'll have to give them a good game. The Roosters have a great squad and deserve to be here so it's going to be a great game to experience."

The Sydney Roosters enter their first grand final for seven years as red-hot favourites against a Newcastle Knights side who have already caused three upsets to make the decider.
It's a grand final that will be historic either way.
The Roosters are either going to break the 50-point curse, or the Knights are going to be the first team in the NRL era to win it all from outside the top four.
The finals series has been something of a roller-coaster for both of these sides, and for the first time in years, the two teams who won their qualifying finals and booked a week off in between that and the grand final qualifier, are out.
The Roosters come into the decider as a side who can put points up in a hurry, but with big questions around their discipline and defensive consistency.
Their run at times this season hasn't resembled that of a side who are going to win the competition, but they have found some real resolve on the run in, and Trent Robinson's side, complete now with Sam Walker back last week in record time from a syndesmosis injury, fired on all cylinders as they put away the Dolphins .
The trip to Brisbane saw the Roosters dominate from start to finish, and win an extra two days in recovery than the Knights, who had to play against the generation's best team in the Penrith Panthers on Sunday afternoon at Homebush.
But that has summed up the Knights' finals campaign.
Grit, determination, a backs to the wall attitude.
That was really never more present than last Sunday as they put together a 46-minute masterclass with 12-men to come from behind and beat the Panthers.
It's why, even as they enter as heavy outsiders for the decider, they can't be written off. Ultimately, the Knights have bought in to what Newcastle is all about, and Justin Holbrook's side have more than enough attacking fizz to do a job, with Kalyn Ponga and Sandon Smith , who has been a revelation since shuffling to halfback, leading the way.
It's actually tough to predict what kind of grand final this will be, with the pace of the game up, both teams able to throw it around and score points, but also with the ability to get into a grind if need be.

items.title: Newcastle Knights’ tale burns bright but Sydney Roosters are built just for NRL’s grand occasion | Jack Snape - The Guardian
items.snippet: Newcastle Knights’ tale burns bright but Sydney Roosters are built just for NRL’s grand occasion | Jack Snape    The Guardian
items.body_excerpt:
Newcastle Knights captain Kalyn Ponga and his Sydney Roosters counterpart James Tedesco pose for a photograph with the Provan-Summons trophy before the 2026 NRL grand final at Accor Stadium. Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAP
Knights’ tale burns bright but Roosters are built just for NRL’s grand occasion
No matter how brilliant Sydney might prove to be on Sunday night, the 2026 grand final will be remembered for Newcastle’s presence in the decider
G rudging favourite the Sydney Roosters meet rugby league’s forgotten child the Newcastle Knights in the NRL grand final on Sunday night. The recipe is delicious, its concoction somehow spiritual: the effect of the combined crossings of every finger in the Hunter Valley, urging just one more win in the Knights’ improbable run to the decider.
Whatever the result, and no matter how brilliant the Roosters might prove to be, the occasion will be remembered for the Knights’ presence. They are, of course, outsiders against the formidable tricolours . The underdogs finished seventh, and the finals have already delivered them three upsets against the Rabbitohs, the Warriors and the Panthers. This Knights’ tale gleams more brightly one year after their wooden spoon.
Sickly sweet and yet of substance, Newcastle’s story keeps giving . The resurrection of coach Justin Holbrook after his assassination on the Gold Coast. Of “better than Lego” , and the demolition of the big penis .
Back then, they were not only the likable battlers from a regional city down on its luck. Andrew Johns and co represented all that was good in the working-class game by rejecting the advances of News Corp’s Super League. Darren Albert’s late try in the 1997 ARL premiership was thus both an on-field triumph and a middle finger upturned towards the breakaway competition and their Hunter Mariners. The Knights then backed it up in 2001 in the modern NRL: a just reward for a team broadly adored, even if by then Matty Johns had moved on.
The TV personality’s prominence in rugby league circles over the past two decades has been the inverse of Knights’ success. Two and a half decades of mediocrity have made mythical those heady but brief Newcastle glories. The club’s broader irrelevance in the intervening period serves as a reminder that opportunities like this do not come around often.
Knights fans greet their team at Martin Place in Sydney. Photograph: Ayush Kumar/Getty Images
Generational? Sunday’s contest is the very definition. The Knights’ first grand final in 25 years is too long ago for Fletcher Sharpe to know what it really means. The five-eighth, 22 years old and the next great playmaker from the Johns’ home town of Cessnock, has to hear about those great Knights teams from his parents, or from much-loved VHS tapes transcoded to now grainy YouTube . A long time coming? Ask Tyson Frizell. No player has waited longer than his 305 NRL games to play their first grand final.
This sudden premiership opportunity feels fragile for those who remember 2001, but many – like young backrowers Jermaine McEwen and Francis Manuleleua, and prop Cody Hopwood – play without the weight of expectation. As fans’ hearts lurch from beat to beat, and “Joey” Johns breaks down in tears, the Knights under Holbrook have proven calm and confident, having knocked off the Warriors in Auckland and now the Panthers with a man down. Behind the quick thinking of half Sandon Smith and his tap against Penrith, and the fearlessness of fullback Kalyn Ponga – epitomised by his destruction of Moses Leota last week – the Knights are fitting partners in Sunday’s dance.
The Roosters, however, are built just for this occasion . The recruitment of veteran half Daly-Cherry Evans, together with the late-career revival of James Tedesco, have aligned perfectly with the emergence of centre Robert Toia and prop Naufahu Whyte, now ripened after a few seasons and both named in the Dally M team of the season.

Talismanic fullbacks Kalyn Ponga and James Tedesco can be gamechangers in the 2026 NRL grand final between the Sydney Roosters and Newcastle Knights. Composite: Getty Images/AAP
NRL 2026 grand final: where the Roosters v Knights decider will be won and lost
It looks to be Sydney’s party, but riding a wave of form and belief Newcastle are primed to crash it with unstoppable force on Sunday
A fter 210 games, 17,000 minutes and more than 10,000 points, it all comes down to the 2026 NRL grand final. One decider. Two desperate teams. The Roosters, a star-studded outfit with four premierships in 25 years and speed, power and tactical brilliance across the park. And the Knights, 25 years without a title and coming off a wooden spoon last year, yet riding an irresistible wave built on blue-collar courage and underdog characters.
The paths to the grand final
The Roosters are hot favourites to win a 16th premiership after compiling a 16-8 win-loss record to finish fourth. Yet, in the final round, they were thrashed 20-50 by their arch-rivals South Sydney and no side has won the NRL title after such a belting. They even dropped their first final to Penrith 12-19 before rebounding to smash the Sharks 46-10 to make the prelim where they flogged the Dolphins 36-20 at Suncorp.
Bradman Best embodies the mood after the Knights’ stunning preliminary final win over the Panthers. Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAP
Newcastle have taken the long way around, finishing with a 14-10 win-loss ledger and scraping into the finals in seventh spot. No team has won the title from there before but the Knights ambushed the Rabbitohs 20-10 at Allianz to make it to the second week, then upset the Warriors 12-10 at Eden Park before a last week’s heroics against the Panthers, defending with 12 men for 44 minutes to triumph 22-14.
The form guide
The emotion of three consecutive boilovers in enemy territory may have drained the Knights. But their form and belief – and the support of the 70,000 Novacastrians expected at Accor Stadium on Sunday – could build them into an unstoppable force. By comparison, the Roosters have cruised into the decider and had an extra day’s rest. It’s their 13th finals campaign in Trent Robinson’s 14 years in charge. They’re calm.
They also have the Knights’ measure, having beaten them in their last six contests and 20 of the past 23. In April, the Chooks won 38-24 despite being 12-24 down at half-time. A five-try second-half blitz led by a double to Mark Nawaqanitawase kept the Knights scoreless for the final 40 minutes. The July rematch was four tries apiece before Daly Cherry-Evans potted a field goal in the 77th minute to steal it 23-22.
The Knights 2025 season was a shocker. They won just six games and collected the wooden spoon. This year, under the cool hand of Justin Holbrook, Newcastle have flipped the fairytale script , averaging 25 points scored and 23 leaked in games this season with captain Kalyn Ponga in the form of his life.
The gamechangers
Cherry-Evans won a premiership in his rookie season with Manly in 2011, but last year dumped the Sea Eagles for the Tricolours to chase another title a record 15 seasons after his first. This will be the 37-year-old’s final NRL game before shipping out to Hull. He will be hoping to echo the feats of another Queensland pivot Cooper Cronk, who led the Roosters to glory in 2018-19.
Mark Nawaqanitawase’s Roosters teammates flock to him after a try in the preliminary final. Photograph: Matt Roberts/Getty Images
In just 46 appearances, Nawaqanitawase has turned himself into the most electric winger in the game, scoring 45 tries, many befitting the all-time highlights reel. This is his last NRL game before rejoining rugby union. The Roosters will be counting on his golden run rolling on, but Knights flyer Dominic Young , an equally brilliant aerial exponent and try-scorer, has the talent to steal his thunder.

Amazingly, they went on to score 3 tries while keeping their opponents scoreless, spurred on by some amazing individual efforts. Leading the way for them was their captain Ponga, who single-handedly reflected the attitude of the team with attacking and defensive displays of brilliance.
